answers_by_date.basis: DL 1.094 (1975), as amended by Ley 18.252 (1983), regulated entry through authorised crossing points (Art. 3) and made clandestine entry a crime (Art. 69). No provision prohibited officers from using force to prevent entry, and no such rule existed in DS 597/1984 or any police statute. No practice evidence was reviewed, since the answer is the lowest option.
The regime was the same as in 2000 (DL 1.094 Arts. 3 and 69). None of the amendments to DL 1.094 between 2000 and 2005 touched the use of force at the border.
No change. Ley 20.430 on refugees was published in April 2010, after this date, and contains no rule on force at the border.

No change. Ley 20.507 (2011) added Art. 33 bis to DL 1.094 and new duties for the Investigations Police (PDI) on identifying people at entry and exit, but said nothing on the use of force against migrants.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been no right protections neither in 2000 nor in 2020

events.what_changed: Sets general guidelines on police use of force when keeping public order: legality, preference for less harmful means, and a warning before firearm use. It does not address preventing migrants from entering, so the answer stays No.

answers.repealed_search: I read the consolidated DL 1.094 (Art. 3 on authorised crossing points, Arts. 68-69 on clandestine entry, Arts. 81 ff. on control measures) and looked for any police or regulatory rule on force at the border between 2000 and 2020. I found no provision, then or later repealed, that prohibited force to prevent entry. The only instrument on force is Decreto 1.364/2018, which is general and covers public order only.
answers.sourcing_note: I read DL 1.094 in its last consolidated version on LeyChile. It shows the amending laws next to each article, and Arts. 3 and 69 were unchanged during 2000-2020. Decreto 1.364 was read on LeyChile. I could not read DS 597/1984.
answers.notes: The answer rests on statutes only. No ruling with a general rule on force at the border was found.

answers_by_date.basis: DL 1.094 had no rule on lethal force at the border; it treated clandestine entry as a crime (Art. 69). No statute or regulation prohibited lethal force to prevent entry.
No change. The general guideline to avoid intentional use of lethal weapons came only with Decreto 1.364 in December 2018, and even that covers public-order operations, not border entry.

answers.repealed_search: I searched DL 1.094 and police use-of-force instruments from 2000 to 2020 for any ban on lethal force against people entering. None was found, and nothing was repealed. Decreto 1.364/2018 is the only instrument on lethal weapons; it is general, limited to public order, and still in force.
answers.sourcing_note: DL 1.094 version history was read on LeyChile, and Decreto 1.364 has a single version. Earlier police use-of-force circulars, which are not norms published on LeyChile, were not read.
answers.notes: Decreto 1.364/2018 may be argued to be a general limit on lethal force. It is confined to public-order interventions and does not mention border entry or migrants, so it was not treated as the protection.

answers_by_date.answer: No, government may punish trafficked or smuggled migrants
answers_by_date.basis: The only trafficking offence was Penal Code Art. 367 bis (Ley 19.409, 1995: facilitating entry or exit for prostitution), with no exemption for victims. DL 1.094 Art. 69 made clandestine entry a crime, and Art. 68 did the same for entry with false documents, with no exception for trafficked or smuggled people. No practice evidence was reviewed (lowest option).

answers_by_date.answer: No, government may punish trafficked or smuggled migrants
answers_by_date.basis: Ley 19.927 (in force 2004-01-14) amended Art. 367 bis to add aggravated penalties but no victim exemption. Ley 19.806 (2002) amended DL 1.094 Art. 68 to bar conditional remission of sentences for false-document entry. Arts. 68-69 still applied to every foreigner.

answers_by_date.answer: No, government may punish trafficked or smuggled migrants
answers_by_date.basis: No change since 2005: Art. 367 bis CP and DL 1.094 Arts. 68-69 in force, no exemption. The 2011 US Trafficking in Persons report confirms that Chilean law before Ley 20.507 covered only cross-border movement for prostitution.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, the national law provides exemption
answers_by_date.basis: Ley 20.507 (in force 2011-04-08) repealed Art. 367 bis and added Penal Code Arts. 411 bis to 411 octies, CPP Art. 78 bis on protecting victims, and DL 1.094 Art. 33 bis (temporary residence for trafficking victims). These are the provisions the 2020 'Yes' rests on. The 2014 US Trafficking in Persons report found 'no reports that the government punished trafficking victims for unlawful acts', but it covers trafficked people only, not smuggled migrants.

answers.change_2000_2020: There was no right protection (as of January 1, 2000), but there is now (as of January 1, 2020)

answers.sourcing_note: I read Ley 20.507 itself, the LeyChile consolidated DL 1.094 with amendment notes, and the Penal Code as of 2010-01-01. The Diario Oficial PDFs and Decreto 42/2005 could not be read. Practice evidence covers trafficking victims about 2013-2014 only; for smuggled migrants and for 2000-2005 there is none.
answers.starting_answer_concern: Ley 20.507 contains no clause exempting trafficked or smuggled migrants from prosecution. It treats them as victims or 'afectados' and gives trafficking victims a residence right (Art. 33 bis), but DL 1.094 Art. 69 (clandestine entry) and Art. 68 (false documents) stayed in force without exception until February 2022. Smuggled migrants could therefore be prosecuted for clandestine entry. On the statutes, the 2020 answer would more accurately be 'No, government may punish trafficked or smuggled migrants'.
answers.notes: The change from 2010 to 2015 follows the starting answer's reliance on Ley 20.507 (in force 8 April 2011); it is not my own reading that the law exempts migrants. The 'Usually' for 2015 rests on the TIP 2014 report, which covers trafficking victims only; nothing was found on whether smuggled migrants were prosecuted under Art. 69, hence low confidence.
